consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same primary identification: 'gnashing of teeth' (in the fixed formula 'weeping and gnashing of teeth') symbolizes the extreme anguish, despair, and remorse of those condemned and excluded at eschatological judgment, conventionally located in hell or final punishment. All responses list, as a common but secondary alternative, the reading that gnashing expresses hostile rage against God or the righteous (citing Psalms 35/37/112, Acts 7:54), and several note minority annihilationist and preterist readings.
book_summary: The book identifies gnashing of teeth as the rage of the wicked directed at the righteous, provoked especially by seeing the kingdom from which they are excluded. It maps the sequence grief–hatred–gnashing–destruction onto Psalm 112:10 and 37:12 and onto Stephen's accusers in Acts 7:54, and it explicitly sets this against the commonly taught view of anguish under conscious, everlasting torment (with 'melt away... perish' implying destruction rather than endless torment).
consensus_core_identification: The anguished, despairing remorse of the condemned suffering conscious eschatological punishment/exclusion (with rage acknowledged only as a secondary alternative nuance).
book_core_identification: Hostile rage of the wicked against the righteous upon seeing the kingdom they are shut out of, following the Psalmic pattern that ends in the wicked's destruction — expressly not the anguish of the damned under everlasting conscious torment.
boundary_disagreement: The book keeps the same gospel occurrences (Matt 8:12; Luke 13:28) but foregrounds the OT/Acts gnashing texts (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Acts 7:54) as the controlling pattern, reclassifying the gospel formula from self-directed anguish/remorse of the tormented to other-directed rage at the righteous, and reclassifying the outcome from ongoing conscious torment to destruction ('melt away... perish').
material_contradiction: The consensus primary reading identifies the emotion as anguish/despair/remorse of the damned within conscious everlasting punishment; the book identifies it as hateful rage at the righteous culminating in the wicked's destruction, and its common-view note explicitly frames the anguish-under-everlasting-torment reading as the view it departs from. Both cannot be the correct identification of the same symbol in the same sense: penitent or despairing self-directed grief under unending torment versus defiant hostility toward the righteous followed by perishing.
rationale: The book does not merely narrow or sharpen the consensus; it replaces the central identification. The consensus core is the anguish of the condemned in conscious eschatological torment. The book's core is the Psalms/Acts pattern of rage against the righteous ending in destruction, and its 'commonly taught' note signals deliberate rejection of the majority reading. Notably, the book's position corresponds to what every blind response lists as a well-known common alternative (rage rather than remorse), so the disagreement is a recognized live dispute — but under this rubric, adopting the alternative against the primary identification, plus the implied denial of everlasting torment, constitutes core contradiction rather than boundary refinement. Extension is partially reclassified: the same Matthean/Lukan texts are retained but read through Psalm 112:10 (see–grieve–gnash–melt away) as a template for Luke 13:28 (see the kingdom–thrust out–gnash).
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: the general referent — the extreme negative reaction of the wicked at exclusion from God's kingdom in the same set of gospel texts — is preserved, and the rage reading is expressly listed by all four responses as a 'common' alternative within the consensus landscape (Response B even folds 'furious anger' into its primary meaning), so the book arguably sits inside the acknowledged interpretive spectrum rather than replacing the referent. Additionally, anguish and rage are not strictly exclusive emotions, weakening the claim of hard contradiction.
